What is the main route of HIV infection in children?
Mother-to-child transmission: during pregnancy, at delivery and through breastfeeding.
What antiretroviral therapy does the mother receive to prevent mother-to-child transmission?
Lifelong dolutegravir-based therapy from the time of diagnosis.
What prophylaxis does a low-risk HIV-exposed infant receive?
What prophylaxis does a high-risk HIV-exposed infant receive?
Zidovudine and nevirapine for 6 weeks; nevirapine continues while the baby is breastfed.
What feeding is advised for an HIV-positive mother on antiretroviral therapy?
Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, then breastfeeding continued with food.
When does an HIV-exposed infant start cotrimoxazole?
From 6 weeks of age until HIV infection is excluded.
Which test diagnoses HIV infection under 18 months of age?
A nucleic acid test (HIV DNA or RNA PCR).
Why is an antibody test not used under 18 months?
Maternal antibody persists for up to 18 months.
When is the first infant PCR done?
At 6 weeks (and also at birth where this is the practice).

Which clinical features suggest HIV infection in a child?
Failure to thrive, persistent oral thrush, recurrent pneumonia, persistent diarrhoea, lymphadenopathy and parotid swelling.
What are the features of Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) in infants?
It occurs at 2–6 months, with severe hypoxia and few chest signs.
